risks: No patients are involved; the risks are overselling one approach and anchoring the committee on an unverified figure.
consent: Not applicable; no patient data are used for the review.
data: Published and publicly available reports only; the spring spot check is described with the department's aggregate figures and no patient identifiers.
equity: PROGRESS-Plus: patients without a primary care clinician, emergency-only patients, patients who need an interpreter and patients in the most deprived neighbourhoods complete follow-up less often. The review extracts results for these groups wherever reported, and the committee report states which approaches were never tested with them.
effectiveness: The committee gets a comparison of approaches with their definitions, settings, resources and blind spots instead of competing single figures.
efficiency: Two radiologists and three librarian days; the review may prevent spending on an approach that misses the patients most at risk.
costs: Staff time within existing roles; no direct costs.
grants: None needed; an evaluation of the chosen approach could later seek hospital quality funding.
partnerships: Hospital librarian, an emergency physician, a primary care representative and a patient partner who comments on how findings should be communicated.
rebPath: A literature review needs no research ethics review; the chair approved it as departmental quality work. Any later evaluation of the chosen approach that uses patient records will go through the hospital's ethics screening.
limitations: Narrative synthesis, English and French reports only, mostly single-centre before-after evidence, and completion definitions that differ.
summary: No participants; the ethical weight lies in honest comparison, attention to the patients most often missed, and keeping unverified figures out.
